Rank them based on, basically there's these four attributes you shared, which I'll actually, I wrote these down. Impact potential, confidence that it will have the impact, clarity of levers and are they differentiated unique levers? Is there something different from what other folks are doing? Those are ways to rank these ideas and problem clusters. You essentially come up with, here's three bets basically we potentially should take. Okay, and then I think that's where you stopped. Is that right?
turns.zh: 好的，这一切都在一周内完成。我知道还有更多。还有一些项目可以帮助您从刚才所说的内容转向下一步，但我喜欢这是该过程中最大元素的核心，您可以在一周内完成，而且由于您提前完成了工作，您只能在一周内完成。再次强调准备步骤的重要性。 (00:39:13)：只是分享您到目前为止所分享的内容，然后我们将完成策略冲刺步骤。它基本上是进行共享，这样每个人都在同一页面上了解所有信息，本质上是所有输入。枚举所有问题，例如单个小问题，然后将它们聚类为 10 到 15 个问题簇。从这里的问题转向这里的机会。对它们进行排名，基本上有你分享的这四个属性，我实际上将它们写下来。影响潜力、对其产生影响的信心、杠杆的清晰度以及它们是否是有差异化的独特杠杆？与其他人做的事情有什么不同吗？这些是对这些想法和问题群进行排序的方法。你基本上会想出，这是我们基本上应该采取的三个赌注。好吧，然后我想你就到此为止了。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: That's totally right, Lenny.
turns.zh: 完全正确，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Those three that are at the top of that pile are basically our strategic pillars. We've sort of gotten our strategic pillars and they basically hold up the strategy. That's why they're called strategic pillars. The idea is once you have the strategic pillars, we basically translate that into a few how might we's? Let's say it's a relevance thing. How might we find the best content for a particular user? How might we surface it in the right place? There's a few how might we's, and the how might we's are basically intended to help the next phase of the process, which is the design sprint. (00:40:43): You generate these areas, these strategic pillars, you generate the how might we's. How might we's are typically pretty straightforward. Once you have the strategic pillars, it takes probably an hour to generate some how might we's for each of them, maybe two or three for each strategic pillar, and then you're done with that stage.
turns.zh: 其中最重要的三个基本上是我们的战略支柱。我们已经找到了战略支柱，它们基本上支撑着我们的战略。这就是为什么它们被称为战略支柱。我们的想法是，一旦有了战略支柱，我们基本上会将其转化为我们可以怎样做？假设这是一个相关性的事情。我们如何为特定用户找到最佳内容？我们如何才能将其显示在正确的位置？我们有一些方法，而我们的方法基本上是为了帮助流程的下一阶段，即设计冲刺。 (00:40:43)：你创造了这些领域、这些战略支柱，你创造了我们的力量。我们如何可能通常非常简单。一旦你有了战略支柱，可能需要一个小时来制定我们对每个战略支柱的建议，也许每个战略支柱有两个或三个，然后你就完成了这个阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just want to highlight real quick, this phrasing is really important. I used exactly the same phrasing. I had a PM that I worked with and his name was Andrew Chen, but not the Andrew Chen people know about, that's an investor, who had this concept of fertile questions that create ideas and spark ideas and solutions. This phrase, "How might we", is actually really powerful as a way to come up with ideas to solve problems. It's just like, how might we increase discoverability in our app? How might we improve relevance? There's something magical about that phrasing that it opens up your mind to, how might we? Let's think about it. Versus like, how do we improve discovery? That's a different, your brain works differently hearing this. That is a really powerful phrasing. Just wanted to highlight that.
turns.zh: 我只是想快速强调一下，这个措辞非常重要。我使用了完全相同的措辞。我有一位与我共事的产品经理，他的名字叫安德鲁·陈（Andrew Chen），但不是人们所知道的安德鲁·陈（Andrew Chen），他是一位投资者，他有这样的概念：提出丰富的问题​​，从而创造想法并激发想法和解决方案。 “我们如何”这句话实际上对于提出解决问题的想法非常有效。就像，我们如何提高应用程序的可发现性？我们如何提高相关性？这句话有一种神奇的魔力，它能打开你的思维，我们可以怎样呢？我们想一想。相比之下，我们如何改进发现？那是不同的，你的大脑听到这个的工作方式会有所不同。这是一个非常有力的措辞。只是想强调这一点。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Yeah, that's awesome. It's also something that designers are familiar with, Lenny, so it flows really well into sort of a design sprint.
turns.zh: 是的，那太棒了。这也是设计师所熟悉的，Lenny，所以它非常适合设计冲刺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you have these how might we'd. You have three pillars, maybe three or four or five how might we's to solve these opportunities/problems, and then what happens after that?
turns.zh: 好吧，既然你有了这些，我们该怎么办呢？你有三个支柱，也许三个、四个或五个，我们如何解决这些机会/问题，然后会发生什么？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly. Then the third day is it's good to start fresh. The team's accomplished a lot.
turns.zh: 确切地。然后第三天就可以重新开始了。该团队取得了很多成就。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This was all the first two days.
turns.zh: 这就是前两天的全部内容。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: This is the first two days, yeah.
turns.zh: 这是前两天，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. So much done in two days.
turns.zh: 哇。好的。两天就做了这么多。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. The second day is particularly intense on the team, so it's good to give them a break, because it's a lot of really mental sort of wrestling, and so give the team a bit of a break. Then the third day is when people are a little bit refreshed, we get to winning aspiration. Winning aspiration is super interesting because it's a very creative exercise. You basically imagine in two years, because that's the typical time horizon of a smaller strategy, is like 18 months to 24 months. This is what I tell the team. Imagine two years there's a newspaper, there's a journalist that covers this work, and there's a newspaper article that comes out. I want you to imagine the progress on all these strategic pillars and what the headline of that newspaper article looks like. It's called a newspaper headline approach. (00:43:09): Basically, everybody generates a newspaper headline in parallel. It's interesting because you often see there's these common themes that sort of form when people generate these headlines. The forcing function with the headline is also that it has to be somewhat simple and plain speak. It's not too technical. You have to get to a more simple layperson's language and you have to get to the key benefit that ultimately, the impact it has on the world. Those kinds of themes come up often. (00:43:44): Then you do a little bit, you put them all into a blender, you put all of those headlines from the team into a blender, and you mash them together and create the winning aspiration, which is ultimately what does progress on the strategy look like in a couple of years time? That comes from the working group, it's not like one person writing.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。第二天对团队来说特别紧张，所以让他们休息一下是件好事，因为这是一场真正的精神角力，所以让团队休息一下。然后第三天，当人们稍微精神一点的时候，我们就开始发愿了。赢得愿望非常有趣，因为这是一项非常有创意的练习。你基本上可以想象两年内的情况，因为这是较小战略的典型时间范围，比如 18 个月到 24 个月。这就是我告诉团队的。想象一下，两年后，有一份报纸，有一位记者报道了这项工作，并发表了一篇报纸文章。我希望你想象一下所有这些战略支柱的进展以及报纸文章的标题是什么样的。这称为报纸标题方法。 (00:43:09)：基本上，每个人都会同时生成报纸标题。这很有趣，因为你经常会看到当人们生成这些标题时，就会形成这些共同的主题。标题的强迫功能还在于它必须简单明了。这不是太技术性的。您必须使用更简单的外行语言，并且必须了解其最终对世界产生的影响的关键好处。这类主题经常出现。 (00:43:44)：然后你做一点，把它们全部放入搅拌机中，将团队中的所有头条新闻放入搅拌机中，然后将它们混合在一起并创造获胜的愿望，这就是几年后战略进展的最终样子？这是工作组出来的，不是一个人写的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of an aspiration that you've come up with on a project you worked on, a winning aspiration?
turns.zh: 您在所从事的项目中提出的愿望（获胜愿望）的例子是什么？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: We did this process for the privacy team when I was at Meta. Really the strategic pillars were around a lot of features that we would build, but the winning aspiration was really like, could we move consumer trust? The newspaper headline is something like, "Facebook has moved the needle on consumer trust by investing in these areas." That's how you create the bigger impact.
turns.zh: 当我在 Meta 时，我们为隐私团队完成了这个过程。实际上，战略支柱是围绕我们将构建的许多功能展开的，但获胜的愿望实际上是，我们能否赢得消费者的信任？报纸的标题是这样的：“Facebook 通过在这些领域进行投资，提高了消费者的信任度。”这就是你创造更大影响的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great example. Obviously this is similar to the PR Amazon method and what I love about your approach, as you said early on, is you're just pulling together all of these awesome ideas from all these different methods of strategy work to a very methodical step-by-step process. Taking all the best ideas into, and as you described, an operator's playbook for doing this. I love that. Okay. When you say blender, by the way, I was thinking as you were talking, put them into a blender, what I'm inferring is you just take everyone's headlines and you come up with one that kind of covers the gamut of all three pillars being successful.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的例子。显然，这与亚马逊的公关方法类似，正如您早些时候所说，我喜欢您的方法的地方在于，您只是将所有这些不同的策略工作方法中的所有这些很棒的想法汇集在一起​​，形成一个非常有条理的逐步过程。正如您所描述的，将所有最好的想法纳入运营商的行动手册中。我喜欢那个。好的。顺便说一句，当你说搅拌机时，我在想，当你说话时，将它们放入搅拌机中，我的推断是，你只需获取每个人的头条新闻，然后你想出一个涵盖所有三个成功支柱的范围。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: That's exactly right. More tactically what I typically do is I put them all on a slide and start, it's almost like a word cloud, and then you start to see these common words. Then you converge those words as the key elements of the final winning aspiration. Then you try to create a nice statement out of that. It also symbolically, everybody sees their own statement on the deck, and that's how you get to the final model.
turns.zh: 完全正确。更具策略性的是，我通常做的是将它们全部放在幻灯片上并开始，它几乎就像一个词云，然后你开始看到这些常见词。然后你将这些词汇聚成最终获胜愿望的关键要素。然后你尝试从中创建一个漂亮的声明。这也具有象征意义，每个人都会在甲板上看到自己的声明，这就是您获得最终模型的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I feel like AI could help with that now.
turns.zh: 惊人的。我觉得人工智能现在可以帮助解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just put in all your headline ideas and it comes up with some suggestions. Okay, cool. Is that the end of the sprint or is there more to the sprint?
turns.zh: 只需输入您所有的标题想法，它就会提出一些建议。好吧，酷。这是冲刺的结束还是冲刺还有更多内容？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: That's it for the sprint.
turns.zh: 这就是冲刺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. At the end of the sprint, what do you have? What are the outputs?
turns.zh: 好的。在冲刺结束时，你有什么？输出是什么？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Yeah, this is a great progress on strategy because now we have the three strategic pillars. We have the how might we associate it with the strategic pillars. You also have the why. Why did you get to those three strategic pillars and what are you not focused on and what are the reasons for it? You also have the winning aspiration. It's great progress. The team's done a great job. I think now we sort of move on to the design sprint.
turns.zh: 是的，这是战略上的巨大进步，因为现在我们有了三大战略支柱。我们知道如何将其与战略支柱联系起来。你也有理由。为什么要实现这三个战略支柱？您没有关注什么？原因是什么？你也有获胜的愿望。这是很大的进步。团队做得很好。我想现在我们可以继续进行设计冲刺了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In your experience, how often are these three the correct three that you end up going with versus you learn something over the course of the rest of the sprint and adjust?
turns.zh: 根据您的经验，这三个是您最终选择的正确三个，而不是您在冲刺的其余部分中学到一些东西并进行调整的频率？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: It's a very good question. We'll speak about an example that I had in Meta where typically during the strategy sprint, you don't change it once you go through the strategy sprint, but eventually there are a lot of signals you get through execution where you sort of have to course correct. We'll talk about one very interesting example of how that sort of changed things here.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常好的问题。我们将讨论我在 Meta 中遇到的一个例子，通常在策略冲刺期间，一旦完成策略冲刺，你就不会更改它，但最终你会在执行过程中收到很多信号，你必须采取正确的方向。我们将讨论一个非常有趣的例子，说明这种情况是如何改变这里的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Basically, you've developed your strategy at this point, and in your experience it ends up being... Until you hit the market and test, you don't really know what's going on.
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。基本上，您此时已经制定了策略，根据您的经验，它最终会...直到您进入市场并进行测试，您才真正知道发生了什么。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But there's kind of an implication that in your experience doing this, I think you said five or six times, it has been correct and as good as doing it any other approach.
turns.zh: 但有一种暗示，根据你这样做的经验，我想你说过五六次，它是正确的，并且与任何其他方法一样好。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: I would say it's not sort of an empirical study, obviously because of the small sample size, but I would say that it's really opened people's eyes and it's led to really good alignment and eventually good results. Even when it has not, it has led to good organizational buy-in on why and how we are approaching things.
turns.zh: 我想说这不是一项实证研究，显然是因为样本量很小，但我想说它确实让人们大开眼界，并且带来了非常好的一致性并最终取得了良好的结果。即使没有，它也导致了组织对我们处理事情的原因和方式的良好支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of, Tomer Cohen was on the podcast, he's CPO of LinkedIn and he has this phrase that always says he says, which is, "We may be wrong, but we're not confused." I love that a core part of this is everyone is completely on the same page, not from the beginning, but once you start this process of here's all the inputs, here's step by step we are working together on narrowing down, so at least everyone understands the why. Which is what sparked your interest in this in the first place, everyone understanding. I know there's a whole rollout at the end too to solve that. (00:48:14): Okay, cool, so we have the sprint. We have basically the three pillars that you're going to invest in, this headline of what it might look like if you're to launch and some solution ideas with how might we's. What comes next?
turns.zh: 这让我想起，Tomer Cohen 在播客中，他是 LinkedIn 的 CPO，他总是说这样一句话，那就是“我们可能错了，但我们并不困惑。”我喜欢这个的核心部分是每个人都完全在同一页面上，而不是从一开始，但是一旦你开始这个过程，这里是所有的输入，这里是我们正在一步一步地缩小范围，所以至少每个人都明白为什么。这首先激发了您对此的兴趣，每个人都理解。我知道最后也会有一个整体的推出来解决这个问题。 (00:48:14)：好的，太酷了，我们开始冲刺了。我们基本上有您要投资的三个支柱，如果您要启动的话，它可能会是什么样子的标题，以及一些我们可以如何做的解决方案想法。接下来会发生什么？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Yeah. The next phase is the design sprint, and the design sprint can be led by the design person who's in the strategy working group. If you remember, there's engineering, product design and data, so the design person can lead it and the PM can sort of take a bit of a backseat during this process. The input to the design sprint is sort of the three strategic pillars and the how might we's associated with it. (00:48:50): The goal of the design sprint is not to sort of come up with these are the features we should build. That's not the purpose of the design sprint. The design sprint is to generate a lot of illustrative concepts that bring the strategy to life because a picture is worth a thousand words. Oftentimes, even though you might have the right words in your strategy doc, people might still scratch their head like, "What do you exactly mean? What are you going to build?" The illustrative concepts really sort of give people something to latch onto, "Oh, okay, I get it. This is what you're going to build at the end of the day with this strategy." (00:49:25): The more generative, the better. Then there's the ability to, sometimes if you do the Google Ventures design sprint, you can even test some of it with users and get a little bit of sharpening of things. The goal here is not to build feature-ready designs, it's more to generate concepts. Once you have that, basically the design sprint, and there's different flavors of design sprints, which I won't go into. You can lean on your design lead to decide what's the appropriate way, but the input and the output is what needs to be very emphasized. The input needs to be the strategic pillars. The output needs to be a ton of illustrative concepts to explain each strategic pillar. You could almost have a section where you talk about each strategic pillar and insert those concepts in that section. That's the idea.
turns.zh: 是的。下一阶段是设计冲刺，设计冲刺可以由战略工作组中的设计人员领导。如果你还记得的话，有工程、产品设计和数据，所以设计人员可以领导它，而项目经理可以在这个过程中退居二线。设计冲刺的输入是三个战略支柱以及我们如何与之相关联。 (00:48:50)：设计冲刺的目标不是想出这些是我们应该构建的功能。这不是设计冲刺的目的。设计冲刺是为了产生大量说明性概念，将策略变为现实，因为一张图片胜过一千个文字。通常，即使你的策略文档中可能有正确的措辞，人们仍然可能会挠头，“你到底是什么意思？你要构建什么？”这些说明性概念确实给了人们一些东西可以抓住，“哦，好吧，我明白了。这就是你在一天结束时用这个策略构建的东西。” (00:49:25)：创造力越强越好。然后，有时如果你进行谷歌风投设计冲刺，你甚至可以与用户一起测试其中的一些内容，并得到一些锐利的东西。这里的目标不是构建功能就绪的设计，而是生成概念。一旦你有了这个，基本上就是设计冲刺，并且有不同风格的设计冲刺，我不会详细讨论。您可以依靠您的设计主管来决定什么是合适的方式，但输入和输出是需要非常强调的。输入需要成为战略支柱。输出需要大量说明性概念来解释每个战略支柱。您几乎可以有一个部分来讨论每个战略支柱并将这些概念插入该部分。就是这个想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to go through a couple examples to make this very real. You mentioned the design sprint method, which we had the authors on the podcast. They actually didn't go through the design sprint method. They have another book called Make Time that's about productivity. We also had their colleague from Google Ventures that designed a bullseye sprint, which is also an interesting sprint. It's a new thing that helps you figure out your ICP and who to focus your product on and how that informs your product.
turns.zh: 我们将通过几个例子来证明这一点。您提到了设计冲刺方法，我们在播客上邀请了作者。他们实际上并没有经历设计冲刺的方法。他们还有另一本书叫《Make Time》，是关于生产力的。我们还有他们谷歌风投的同事设计了一个牛眼冲刺，这也是一个有趣的冲刺。这是一个新事物，可以帮助您确定您的 ICP、您的产品的重点对象以及如何通知您的产品。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Oh, that's right. Interesting.
turns.zh: 哦，是这样。有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's another type of sprint you could use here. The input is here's the three things we're going to invest in, say discovery, relevance, privacy. The output is here's concepts of what this could look like to get people's minds going. Is it just a bunch of mocks basically in a deck at this point?
turns.zh: 这是您可以在此处使用的另一种冲刺类型。输入的是我们要投资的三件事，即发现、相关性、隐私。输出是这样的概念，即这可能会是什么样子，以激发人们的思维。现在这只是套牌中的一堆模拟吗？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: That's correct. Yeah.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Okay, amazing. That's a week. That's another sprint. PM could maybe take a little bit of a break.
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。好吧，太棒了。那是一个星期。那是另一次冲刺。首相也许可以稍微休息一下。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And designers take the lead.
turns.zh: 设计师起带头作用。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The engineers are kind of inputs and thought partners in this, I imagine.
turns.zh: 我想，工程师们是这方面的投入者和思想伙伴。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: They're optional. Yeah.
turns.zh: 它们是可选的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Optional, but yeah, ideally they're involved because you want all the best ideas in there.
turns.zh: 可选，但是，是的，理想情况下他们会参与其中，因为你希望其中包含所有最好的想法。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. What comes next?
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。接下来会发生什么？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Then the next step is the document writing. This is sort of a solo activity that the PM should take on, but the great news is the PM is not starting from scratch. There's so much great stuff to write. If you remember, there's a ton of user insights, a ton of behavioral insights, a ton of competitive analysis. There's the three strategic pillars, how might we's, winning aspiration. There's a whole bunch of illustrative concepts. (00:51:48): Oftentimes, product leads have this sort of creator's block. That is solved here completely because you have a ton of great material. I have to tell you, it doesn't make the job easier. You still have to weave together a good story. That's why I think it takes a week or two. I think it's really about combining, connecting and editing at this point and telling a cohesive story from all those components, but I think the building blocks are really solid and defensible.
turns.zh: 然后下一步就是文档写作。这是总理应该承担的一项单独活动，但好消息是总理并不是从头开始。有很多很棒的东西要写。如果你还记得的话，有大量的用户洞察、大量的行为洞察、大量的竞争分析。有三个战略支柱，我们如何才能赢得愿望。有一大堆说明性概念。 (00:51:48)：产品负责人常常会遇到这种创作者的障碍。这个问题在这里得到了彻底解决，因为你有大量很棒的材料。我必须告诉你，这并不会让工作变得更容易。你仍然需要编织一个好故事。这就是为什么我认为需要一两周的时间。我认为这实际上是关于在这一点上进行组合、连接和编辑，并从所有这些组件中讲述一个有凝聚力的故事，但我认为构建块确实是坚固且可靠的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a template or kind of sections you like to include in your strategy doc? As someone sits down and is trying to write this out, what do you want to see there as headings?
turns.zh: 您是否希望在策略文档中包含模板或某些部分？当有人坐下来试图写下这个内容时，您希望看到什么作为标题？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: I think you could almost take the building blocks as a little bit of a steer for the template. You start with the broader context where you talk about what the leaders kind of want from this overall effort. Then you get into key insights and analysis where you have user insights, behavioral insights, competitive analysis. Then you get into the strategic pillars and you explain them. You also explain why. In the appendix, you include the full table that you generated on day two of your strategy sprint. You include the full table in the appendix, including the criteria. That's going to be really important because most people are going to ask, "Why did you pick these?" That's basically sort of the defensibility. (00:53:17): Then you have the winning aspiration that's very bold. It's a big part of the heart of the deck, and you sort of embed the illustrative concepts into the actual each of the strategic pillars so that it flows well. Then finally, you end with some kind of alignment questions like, "Hey, do these feel right? Are there things we are missing?" So that it creates that framework for alignment in the subsequent meetings.
turns.zh: 我认为您几乎可以将构建块视为模板的一点指导。你从更广泛的背景开始，谈论领导者希望从整体努力中得到什么。然后你会进入关键的洞察和分析，其中有用户洞察、行为洞察、竞争分析。然后你进入战略支柱并解释它们。你也解释一下原因。在附录中，您将包含在策略冲刺第二天生成的完整表格。您可以在附录中包含完整的表格，包括标准。这非常重要，因为大多数人都会问：“你为什么选择这些？”这基本上就是防御性。 (00:53:17)：那么你就有非常大胆的获胜愿望。它是这套牌核心的重要组成部分，你可以将说明性概念嵌入到实际的每个战略支柱中，以便它能够很好地流动。最后，你会以某种一致性问题结束，例如，“嘿，这些感觉对吗？我们是否遗漏了一些东西？”这样它就可以为后续会议中的协调创建框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to chat with Christina Gilbert, the founder of OneSchema, one of our longtime podcast sponsors. Hi, Christina.
turns.zh: 我很高兴能与 OneSchema 的创始人 Christina Gilbert 聊天，OneSchema 是我们的长期播客赞助商之一。嗨，克里斯蒂娜。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Yes. Thank you for having me on, Lenny.
turns.zh: 是的。谢谢你邀请我参加，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the latest with OneSchema? I know you now work with some of my favorite companies, like Ramp, Vanta, Scale and Watershed. I heard that you just launched a new product.
turns.zh: OneSchema 的最新动态是什么？我知道您现在与一些我最喜欢的公司合作，例如 Ramp、Vanta、Scale 和 Watershed。我听说你们刚刚推出了一款新产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... and to scale and watershed, I heard that you just launched a new product to help product teams import CSVs from especially tricky systems like ERPs.
turns.zh: ...就规模和分水岭而言，我听说你们刚刚推出了一款新产品，帮助产品团队从 ERP 等特别棘手的系统导入 CSV。

turns.speaker: Christina
turns.en: Yes, so we just launched one scheme of file feeds, which allows you to build an integration with any system in 15 minutes, as long as you can export a CSV to an SFTP folder. (00:54:18): We see our customers all the time getting stuck with hacks and workarounds, and the product teams that we work with don't have to turn down prospects because their systems are too hard to integrate with. We allow our customers to offer thousands of without involving their engineering team at all.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我们刚刚推出了一种文件源方案，只要您可以将 CSV 导出到 SFTP 文件夹，您就可以在 15 分钟内与任何系统构建集成。 (00:54:18)：我们看到我们的客户总是陷入黑客攻击和解决方法的困境，而与我们合作的产品团队不必因为他们的系统太难集成而拒绝潜在客户。我们允许客户提供数千种产品，而无需他们的工程团队参与。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to be able to take this off my roadmap, and instead use something like OneSchema, and not just to build it, but also to maintain it forever?
turns.zh: 我可以告诉您，如果我的团队必须构建这样的集成，那么如果能够将其从我的路线图上删除，并使用 OneSchema 之类的东西，并且不仅要构建它，而且要永远维护它，那该有多好？

turns.speaker: Christina
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of multi-day outages from even just a handful of bad records. We are laser focused on integration reliability to help teams end all of those distractions that come up with integrations. (00:54:55): We have a built-in validation layer that stops any bad data from entering your system, and OneSchema will notify your team immediately of any data that looks incorrect.
turns.zh: 当然，莱尼。我们已经听过许多因少数不良记录而导致多天停电的恐怖故事。我们高度关注集成可靠性，以帮助团队消除集成带来的所有干扰。 (00:54:55)：我们有一个内置的验证层，可以阻止任何不良数据进入您的系统，并且 OneSchema 会立即通知您的团队任何看起来不正确的数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Christina, thank you for joining us, and if you want to learn more, head on over to oneschema.co. That's oneschema.co. (00:55:17): I pulled up Playing to Win, which I know you also pull ideas from, and actually Roger Martin was on the podcast talking about this stuff. And one way I think about it as you're describing a way to break up your strategy doc, is he has these five questions that you ask. (00:55:31): The first is actually what's your winning aspiration? So I love that you're pulling that in. This is one approach your doc would be. What's your winning aspiration? Where will you play? What market are you going after? How will you win? What capabilities must be in place for you to win? And then what management systems are required? (00:55:46): We'll link to this framework just in case people want that as a crutch in their thinking strategy, but is there anything that we could link folks to that describe how you like to think about this doc? And if not, it'd be cool if you make a template that folks could borrow.
turns.zh: 我知道导入不正确的数据会给您的客户带来各种痛苦，并很快失去他们的信任。克里斯蒂娜，感谢您加入我们，如果您想了解更多信息，请访问 oneschema.co。那是 oneschema.co。 (00:55:17)：我打开了《Playing to Win》，我知道你也从中汲取了想法，实际上罗杰·马丁（Roger Martin）在播客上谈论了这些东西。当你描述一种分解你的策略文档的方法时，我想到的一个方法是，他有你问的这五个问题。 (00:55:31)：第一个问题是你的获胜愿望是什么？所以我喜欢你把它拉进来。这是你的医生会采取的一种方法。你的获胜愿望是什么？你会去哪里玩？你要追求什么市场？你将如何获胜？您必须具备哪些能力才能获胜？那么需要什么样的管理系统呢？ (00:55:46)：我们将链接到这个框架，以防万一人们希望将其作为他们的思维策略中的拐杖，但是我们是否可以将人们链接到描述您如何看待此文档的内容？如果没有，如果您制作一个人们可以借用的模板，那就太酷了。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: I'm happy to share of the flowchart of the process and the template as well.
turns.zh: 我很高兴分享该流程的流程图和模板。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So this is how long of a process, this writing of the document?
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。那么这个文档的编写需要多长时间的过程呢？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: It's about one to two weeks, and I think it's mostly solo work and hopefully by the end of it there's a very tight doc, and that's what we use to roll out.
turns.zh: 大约需要一到两周的时间，我认为这主要是个人工作，希望到最后会有一个非常紧凑的文档，这就是我们用来推出的内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And by solo work, I imagine you're looping in this working team to get their feedback as you're pulling it together, or is it just you sit there in a room and then...
turns.zh: 通过单独工作，我想你在这个工作团队中循环以获取他们的反馈，因为你把它放在一起，或者只是你坐在一个房间里，然后......

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: I would minimize pulling them in, because they've all contributed so much to the process already. So, I would say that at the end of it, obviously, once you have a draft, it's good to share with them, but I wouldn't tap their cycles too much at this point, because they've given a lot already.
turns.zh: 我会尽量减少他们的参与，因为他们都已经为这个过程做出了很大的贡献。所以，我想说，最后，显然，一旦你有了草案，与他们分享是件好事，但此时我不会过多利用他们的周期，因为他们已经付出了很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. Okay. (00:56:48): And how many pages do you see this doc being, roughly? What's a heuristic?
turns.zh: 我懂了。好的。 (00:56:48)：您认为这份文档大约有多少页？什么是启发式？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: It's not too long. I would say probably three or four pages and then an appendix has a lot of additional... Like, the table I spoke about and a lot of additional maybe illustrative concepts. Maybe you can only use a few illustrative concepts in the main section so that there could be others there. (00:57:09): I think usually there's a desire from leaders to say, "Okay, what are we building next?" And it's important not to include a roadmap as part of a strategy doc, because a strategy doc is meant to be separate from the roadmap. It's meant to be a companion to your roadmap. And even though there's interest, maybe sometimes you can include a illustrative roadmap in the appendix, but I would try to keep it clean and try to keep it focused on just the strategy.
turns.zh: 时间并不太长。我想说可能是三到四页，然后附录有很多额外的……就像我谈到的表格和很多额外的可能说明性的概念。也许您只能在主要部分中使用一些说明性概念，以便可以有其他概念。 (00:57:09)：我认为领导者通常会说：“好吧，我们下一步要建设什么？”重要的是不要将路线图作为战略文档的一部分，因为战略文档应该与路线图分开。它旨在成为您的路线图的伴侣。即使有兴趣，也许有时您可以在附录中包含说明性路线图，但我会尽力保持其简洁并尝试使其仅关注策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So at this point you basically developed your strategy, the next step, I think you call rollout, where you just start actually rolling this out, so let's talk about that. But it's important to note how many weeks in this is. This is like six-ish weeks of work and you've got a strategy for your company/product?
turns.zh: 所以在这一点上，你基本上制定了你的策略，下一步，我认为你称之为推出，你刚刚开始实际推出它，所以让我们来谈谈。但重要的是要注意这有多少周。这就像六周左右的工作，您已经为您的公司/产品制定了策略吗？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: That's exactly right. So I think you're probably in the last two to three weeks of the process, and pretty important final step is the rollout, and I would start with what I call gatekeepers. And these are people who are absolutely... You have to get their one-on-one alignment and blessing on this before it moves forward. And it's probably not too many, probably two or three people. So I would pre-flight it with them and get their alignment.
turns.zh: 完全正确。因此，我认为您可能处于该过程的最后两到三周，非常重要的最后一步是推出，我将从我所说的“看门人”开始。这些人绝对是……在事情向前发展之前，你必须得到他们的一对一的协调和祝福。而且人数可能不会太多，大概两三个人。所以我会和他们一起进行预飞行并让他们对齐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So these are one-on-one meetings with these gatekeepers?
turns.zh: 那么这些是与这些看门人的一对一会议吗？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: These are one-on-one meetings. Exactly. (00:58:31): And then there's a larger group of what I call key stakeholders, people who are impacted by it, different functional leaders, et cetera. And that can be done either async or through a group review. And then there's probably a rolling of list of team roadshows. There's different ways to do this, but the one that I feel is most effective is the roadshow where you have about eight to 10 people in each session, so people feel more comfortable to ask questions and it's more conversational. (00:59:06): So the purpose of this stage is to land it. It's not to seek too much feedback, so it's a delicate balance. At the same time, you don't want to appear just being too inflexible. So it's a very delicate balance. When people ask questions, you can clarify it, and you can add clarifications to the doc, but I wouldn't change... The most important thing, three strategic pillars, I wouldn't change that. I would defend it using the framework, but if people are like, "there's really good arguments about the criteria that led to your ranking," then it's okay to reconsider it. I've not seeing it happen in my five to six attempts, but it's possible, theoretically possible.
turns.zh: 这些是一对一的会议。确切地。 (00:58:31)：然后还有一个更大的群体，我称之为关键利益相关者、受其影响的人、不同的职能领导者等等。这可以异步完成，也可以通过小组评审完成。然后可能会有一系列团队路演列表。有不同的方法可以做到这一点，但我认为最有效的方法是路演，每次会议大约有 8 到 10 个人，这样人们会更舒服地提出问题，而且更具对话性。 (00:59:06)：所以这个阶段的目的是落地。并不是寻求太多的反馈，所以这是一个微妙的平衡。同时，您也不希望显得过于僵化。所以这是一个非常微妙的平衡。当人们提出问题时，你可以澄清它，你可以在文档中添加澄清，但我不会改变......最重要的事情，三个战略支柱，我不会改变这一点。我会使用这个框架来捍卫它，但如果人们会说，“对于导致你的排名的标准确实有很好的论据”，那么就可以重新考虑它。我在五到六次尝试中没有看到这种情况发生，但这是可能的，理论上是可能的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The core of this approach it sounds like, is you've done a lot of the pre-work where you land in a generally correct place. (00:59:55): Okay, so this is the rollout. So what I'm thinking as you talk, say you're like a PM on a team, say you're working on privacy, it's like an IC, your ICPM, working on strategy. How do you think about including, say, your manager because through this process, when do you start to like, "Hey, here's what we're planning, here's what we're thinking," making sure they're on board? Because I could see this working team off to the side working, working, working. "Okay, we're ready to roll it out." Oftentimes there's like, "No, wait. There's all this other stuff happening at the company, we don't have resources." Where do you loop them in? How do you think about that kind of stakeholder?
turns.zh: 听起来，这种方法的核心是，您已经完成了大量的前期工作，从而到达了大致正确的位置。 (00:59:55)：好的，这就是发布。所以当你说话时我在想什么，假设你就像一个团队的 PM，假设你正在研究隐私，它就像一个 IC，你的 ICPM，正在研究策略。你如何考虑让你的经理参与其中，因为通过这个过程，你什么时候开始喜欢，“嘿，这就是我们正在计划的，这就是我们正在思考的，”确保他们参与其中？因为我可以看到这个工作团队在一旁工作、工作、工作。 “好的，我们已经准备好推出它了。”通常情况下，“不，等等。公司里发生了所有其他事情，我们没有资源。”你把它们循环到哪里？您如何看待这种利益相关者？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: The the more attuned PMs who understand organizational dynamics, probably keep the manager pretty in sync through the process. I think, definitely, the manager becomes a person who you interview as part of the leadership interviews, so you know what the manager's looking for from the effort. (01:00:49): And then once you get to the strategic pillars on day two of the strategy sprint, you probably want to just quickly pre-flight it with the manager and say, "Hey, look, this is how it's trending, and these are the things we are probably not going to do" and any issues with that. And then eventually you actually want your manager to support you in some of these bigger meetings, so you enlist their help. So I would say that it's probably each individual style, but I would keep them pretty aligned through the process. But you don't have to be too heavy [inaudible 01:01:23], just be super light.
turns.zh: PM 越了解组织动态，就越能在整个过程中与经理保持同步。我认为，经理肯定会成为你在领导力面试中面试的人，所以你知道经理从努力中寻找什么。 (01:00:49)：一旦你在战略冲刺的第二天到达战略支柱，你可能只想快速与经理一起进行预检，并说：“嘿，看，这就是趋势，这些是我们可能不会做的事情”以及与此相关的任何问题。最终，您实际上希望您的经理在一些大型会议中为您提供支持，因此您寻求他们的帮助。所以我想说，这可能是每个人的风格，但我会让它们在整个过程中保持一致。但你不必太重 [听不清 01:01:23]，只需超轻即可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. Makes a lot of sense to me. There's like a... (01:01:26): We're not going to solve everyone's problems with this one framework, maybe just quickly touch on resourcing. As you think about this. Like a part of a strategy includes like, oh, we also need these resources. Just any thoughts on how to include that? And then I want to get into some examples of how you've actually implemented this.
turns.zh: 伟大的。对我来说很有意义。就像... (01:01:26)：我们不会用这个框架解决每个人的问题，也许只是快速触及资源问题。当你想到这一点时。就像战略的一部分包括这样，哦，我们也需要这些资源。关于如何包含它有什么想法吗？然后我想通过一些例子来说明您是如何实际实现这一点的。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: So I actually don't recommend thinking about resources in the strategy phase, because what you're saying is, "these are the areas of focus" and the resourcing question becomes more relevant from a road mapping standpoint. (01:01:55): Because then you say, "Okay, what percentage of our engineering do we put on strategic pillar A, versus B, versus C? And what are the specific things we build?" So it becomes a road-mapping question as opposed to a strategy question.
turns.zh: 所以我实际上不建议在战略阶段考虑资源，因为你所说的是，“这些是重点领域”，从路线图的角度来看，资源问题变得更加相关。 (01:01:55)：因为你会说，“好吧，我们在战略支柱 A、B、C 上投入了多少比例的工程？我们构建的具体内容是什么？”因此，它变成了一个路线图问题，而不是一个战略问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so by the end of this, the rollout, the part of the rollout is developing the actual roadmap. We're not going to get deep into that. That could be part two, solve every PM's problems, teach them all the steps of the process, but we're going to cut it off at, here's you have a strategy that is starting to be rolled out.
turns.zh: 因此，到了推广结束时，推广的一部分就是制定实际的路线图。我们不会深入探讨这一点。这可能是第二部分，解决每个产品经理的问题，教他们流程的所有步骤，但我们将在以下时间结束，这是一个正在开始推出的策略。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. (01:02:25): Let's go through a couple examples where you actually move into this to make this even more real. I know there's a couple companies you were thinking about sharing, strategies you worked on.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。 (01:02:25)：让我们看几个例子，在这些例子中你实际上会进入这个领域，让这变得更加真实。我知道您正在考虑分享几家公司的工作策略。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: I think there's just three quick notes to close off this process and I'll share two examples, Lenny.
turns.zh: 我认为只需三个简短的说明即可结束此过程，我将分享两个例子，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美的。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: So the reason I think this process works, the first is because there is a ton of alignment built in within team alignment and leadership alignment built in. And it's not seen as, "Oh, this PM went off and wrote this strategy doc and I don't agree with most of it." And part of this is actually very... (01:03:09): It goes back to human psychology of just something that comes from you, feels a lot more familiar and easy to accept. So this doc is actually not from the PM, the PM is facilitating it, but it's actually from the strategy working group. And the strategy working group are the leads of the team. And so it's actually... And the leadership inputs have been baked in, so it's actually very team representative. And so hopefully there isn't too much misalignment when you roll it out. And I have seen that, I've seen that work out. (01:03:43): The second is there's just better results. You get to better problem articulation, you get a better strategic pillar, because there's just more minds on it than if it was just a product lead. (01:03:55): And the third thing is you have clearly defensible criteria and outputs, and if you want to change it, like I said, you have to go back to the criteria and the scoring and then say, "Okay, why do we believe this has to be changed?" And even a change is easy to justify once you do that. So it creates a lot of benefits, but ultimately, and we'll get to this a little bit more, it has to be tested with execution, and that's the most important thing.
turns.zh: 所以我认为这个流程有效的原因，首先是因为团队协调和领导层协调中内置了大量的协调。而且它不会被视为“哦，这位产品经理写了这份战略文档，而我不同意其中的大部分内容。”其中一部分实际上非常... (01:03:09)：这可以追溯到人类心理学，即来自你的东西，感觉更熟悉且更容易接受。所以这个文档实际上不是来自 PM，PM 正在推动它，但它实际上来自战略工作组。战略工作组是团队的领导者。所以它实际上......领导层的投入已经融入其中，所以它实际上非常具有团队代表性。所以希望当你推出它时不会有太多的错位。我已经看到了这一点，我已经看到了这一点。 (01:03:43)：第二个是有更好的结果。你可以更好地阐明问题，你可以得到更好的战略支柱，因为与产品领导相比，有更多的人在思考它。 (01:03:55)：第三件事是你有明确的可辩护的标准和输出，如果你想改变它，就像我说的，你必须回到标准和评分，然后说，“好吧，为什么我们认为必须改变它？”一旦你这样做了，即使是改变也很容易被证明是合理的。所以它创造了很多好处，但最终，我们将进一步讨论这一点，它必须通过执行进行测试，这是最重要的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's important to highlight, no framework playbook [inaudible 01:04:26] method is going to guarantee you have the correct strategy that will win and your company will thrive. It's always just the best effort at plan. (01:04:35): As the quote, "no good plan survives first contact with the customer."
turns.zh: 我认为重要的是要强调，没有任何框架剧本 [听不清 01:04:26] 方法可以保证您拥有能够获胜并且您的公司能够蓬勃发展的正确策略。这始终只是计划中的最大努力。 (01:04:35)：正如引用的那样，“没有好的计划能够在与客户的第一次接触中幸存下来。”

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Let's talk through some examples.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。让我们通过一些例子来讨论。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: so the first example I wanted to talk about is at Zynga. I was at Zynga a very long time ago, and this was the heyday of social gaming on Facebook. The thing that I was extremely impressed about Zynga was the strategic clarity and strategic encoding at the company. And this was not attributable to me, by the way, this was already there when I got there as a entry-level PM, but the kind of strategic clarity there was really, really impressive and it was very evident and observable from all the games. (01:05:22): So if you look at all the games, there were three elements that were very common across all the games. The first was viral game loops. There's these game loops that just required you to have a social and active social network to be successful and play, and it was very tightly and fictionally integrated into the core of the gameplay. That was the first one. (01:05:47): The second one was there was this idea of paying to complete things. So you're not paying to skip a whole experience, what you're paying is just to complete it. So what happens then is different people, depending on how much time they have, complete different percentages of a progression task, or a part of the gameplay, and you only had to pay the rest to get through the experience. And it was this interesting experience where people put a lot of investment into it, and they didn't mind paying for the last 20% or 30%, which was very interesting, because it created this market for different elasticity of spend, different times that people had in their lives. And it was very, very clever. So that was again, very common across all the games. (01:06:38): And then the third was network. So all of Zynga games had this cross-promotional component at the top of the game and they would promote other games, and it's like the Zynga network was the most important thing, and not an individual game. And those were the three in our parlance now strategic pillars, and there were non-focus areas. It wasn't like... (01:07:05): The focus wasn't on high-fidelity graphics, it wasn't on complex game mechanics, and this was extremely clear and hard-coded into the company culture and operations. And it was perfectly tuned to the environment at the time. Facebook platform afforded strong support with social graph, and channels, and basically the game studios contributed through different games in a very network accretive way. (01:07:31): So for example, I was at Zynga San Diego, and we took the company into net new game genres like action strategy, match three puzzle games, but we stayed true to the strategic pillars of the company, and we had to invent new mechanics so that the strategic pillars would work in the new genres that we introduced to the company. And what was fascinating is the company actually had systems to reinforce these strategic pillars. (01:07:57): And, for example, the data infrastructure was very incredible at the time, and really reinforced these strategic pillars. There was this function called Central Product Management, which basically propagated best practices, made sure that games were network accretive and all these things worked in harmony to enhance those strategic pillars and reinforce it, and it worked really well. The company, if I remember right, got to a billion dollars, it was the fastest to get to a billion dollars in the history of companies at the time.
turns.zh: 所以我想讲的第一个例子是 Zynga。很久以前我在 Zynga 工作，当时正是 Facebook 社交游戏的鼎盛时期。 Zynga 给我留下深刻印象的是该公司的战略清晰度和战略编码。顺便说一句，这并不是我的功劳，当我作为初级产品经理到达那里时，这已经存在了，但是那里的战略清晰度确实非常令人印象深刻，并且从所有游戏中都非常明显和可观察到。 (01:05:22)：如果你观察所有游戏，就会发现所有游戏中都存在三个非常常见的元素。第一个是病毒式游戏循环。这些游戏循环只需要你拥有一个社交和活跃的社交网络才能成功并玩游戏，并且它非常紧密且虚构地融入到游戏玩法的核心中。这是第一个。 (01:05:47)：第二个是付费来完成事情的想法。因此，您付费并不是为了跳过整个体验，而是为了完成它。那么接下来会发生的情况是，不同的人，根据他们有多少时间，完成不同百分比的进度任务，或者游戏的一部分，而你只需要支付剩余的费用来完成体验。正是这种有趣的经历，人们投入了大量的投资，而且他们不介意为最后的 20% 或 30% 买单，这非常有趣，因为它为人们生活中不同的支出弹性、不同的时间创造了这个市场。这非常非常聪明。所以这在所有游戏中都很常见。 (01:06:38)：第三个是网络。因此，所有 Zynga 游戏在游戏顶部都有这种交叉推广组件，他们会推广其他游戏，就好像 Zynga 网络才是最重要的，而不是单个游戏。这些就是我们现在所说的三个战略支柱，并且存在非重点领域。它不像... (01:07:05)：重点不在于高保真图形，也不在于复杂的游戏机制，而且这一点非常清晰并硬编码到公司文化和运营中。而且非常符合当时的环境。 Facebook 平台通过社交图谱和渠道提供了强有力的支持，基本上游戏工作室通过不同的游戏以一种非常网络增值的方式做出了贡献。 (01:07:31)：例如，我在 Zynga 圣地亚哥，我们将公司带入全新的游戏类型，例如动作策略、三消益智游戏，但我们坚持公司的战略支柱，我们必须发明新的机制，以便战略支柱能够在我们向公司引入的新类型中发挥作用。令人着迷的是，该公司实际上拥有加强这些战略支柱的系统。 (01:07:57)：例如，当时的数据基础设施非常令人难以置信，并且确实强化了这些战略支柱。有一个称为中央产品管理的功能，它基本上传播最佳实践，确保游戏具有网络增值性，所有这些东西协调一致地增强和强化这些战略支柱，而且效果非常好。如果我没记错的话，这家公司达到了10亿美元，是当时公司历史上最快达到10亿美元的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In revenue.
turns.zh: 在收入方面。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: In revenue. (01:08:35): And it worked really well until the environment changed and there was a shift to mobile. And temporarily... Basically, if you go back to that resonance concept, that deep resonance between the product and the market was temporarily lost once that shift happened to mobile.
turns.zh: 在收入方面。 (01:08:35)：它的效果非常好，直到环境发生变化并转向移动设备。暂时......基本上，如果你回到那个共鸣概念，一旦这种转变发生在移动领域，产品和市场之间的深刻共鸣就会暂时消失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's a lot here. I think one interesting note here is, as you said, the strategy work you're doing, which sounds like a lot of time, eight to 12 weeks potentially, this lasted a long time for Zynga. And so I think it's important to remember the work you're doing here, even though... (01:09:06): On the one hand it feels like a long time, on the other hand, it feels like very little time to come up with the things that will most help your business grow. In this case, these three elements for Zynga. And by the way, these three pillars, they didn't emerge from this method, but it helped you see the power of being very clear...
turns.zh: 所以这里有很多东西。我认为这里一个有趣的注释是，正如您所说，您正在做的战略工作，这听起来像是很长的时间，可能需要 8 到 12 周，这对 Zynga 来说持续了很长时间。因此，我认为记住您在这里所做的工作很重要，尽管... (01:09:06)：一方面感觉时间很长，另一方面感觉时间很少，无法想出最能帮助您的业务发展的事情。在本例中，这三个要素适用于 Zynga。顺便说一句，这三个支柱，它们不是从这个方法中出现的，但它帮助你看到了非常清晰的力量......

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Clear, exactly.
turns.zh: 清楚，准确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And having everything centered around, we all agree, these are the three ways we win. Okay, cool. And then I think the number three, again, I just want to highlight the power of just very few bets in investments. So it's always three. I've always suggested three as well. Some people are like, "three to five," but I think it's... You just find, in general, three is the right number as much? Try very, very hard to make it three?
turns.zh: 我们都同意，一切以一切为中心，这是我们获胜的三种方式。好吧，酷。然后我想再次强调第三点，我只是想强调投资中很少下注的力量。所以总是三。我也一直建议三个。有些人会说“三到五”，但我认为......你发现，一般来说，三是正确的数字？努力非常非常努力地做到三个？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: I agree.
turns.zh: 我同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. (01:09:48): And then I think there's also this element of differentiation being really important. So these three elements you shared for Zynga are just like they're unique and differentiated for Zynga. Network, powers of apps driving other apps, paying to complete, these are things Zynga has figured out, "this is how we" win versus other products in the market.
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。 (01:09:48)：然后我认为这种差异化元素也非常重要。因此，您为 Zynga 分享的这三个元素对于 Zynga 来说是独一无二且与众不同的。网络、应用程序驱动其他应用程序的能力、付费完成这些都是 Zynga 已经弄清楚的，“这就是我们”战胜市场上其他产品的方式。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Anything else along those lines with Zynga?
turns.zh: 甜的。 Zynga 还有其他类似的事情吗？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: That was in hindsight reflection, Lenny, I was pretty naive when I was there, and I realized how... And this was, in fact, what led to my blind spot when I joined Headspace from Zynga, that you even need a strategy. That's the story I said at the beginning. (01:10:33): The reason is because Zynga had it figured out so well that I didn't actually have a need to exercise that muscle at Zynga, and we just had to come up with new games that applied that strategy. And so it was a net new muscle I had to develop when I got to Headspace.
turns.zh: 这是事后反思，Lenny，我在那里的时候非常天真，我意识到......事实上，这就是当我从 Zynga 加入 Headspace 时导致我的盲点的原因，你甚至需要一个策略。这就是我一开始说的故事。 (01:10:33)：原因是 Zynga 已经把它弄清楚得非常好，以至于我实际上不需要在 Zynga 锻炼这种能力，我们只需想出应用该策略的新游戏即可。因此，当我到达顶空时，这是我必须发展的新肌肉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like that parable of the fish swimming in the water where the older fish swims by and he's like, "How's the water?" And they're like, "Hmm?" And then he leaves and he's like, "What's water?" You just don't realize what you're in. You don't realize what you're surrounded by until it's gone.
turns.zh: 这就像鱼在水里游泳的寓言，老鱼游过，他问，“水怎么样？”他们就像，“嗯？”然后他离开了，他问：“水是什么？”你只是没有意识到你身处什么。你没有意识到你被什么包围着，直到它消失。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one other thing I just want to highlight while we're on this topic is just the power of focus. In the case of Zynga, just this focus on everything we do needs to get these things, these three things, everything we do, we need to do in order to win. And I think that's a recurring theme in what you're talking about, is just focus. The steps of the process are focus on this one part for now. So I think that's a really interesting thread is just the power of focus.
turns.zh: 当我们谈论这个话题时，也许我想强调的另一件事就是专注的力量。就 Zynga 而言，我们所做的一切都需要专注于这些事情，这三件事，我们所做的一切，我们需要做的事情才能获胜。我认为这是你所谈论的一个反复出现的主题，就是焦点。该过程的步骤目前主要集中在这一部分。所以我认为这是一个非常有趣的线索，就是专注的力量。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. (01:11:35): And now you have another example of your time at Meta.
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。 (01:11:35)：现在您又可以看到您在 Meta 的经历的另一个例子。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: At Meta there's this fascinating example, which I think illustrates a different point, which is... (01:11:46): Basically I was standing up the product strategy for a couple of product growth teams in Reality Labs, Oculus, which was coming up with the Quest II at the time. This is a standalone headset, and then Portal, which was our video conferencing product. And we stood up these teams to go after product growth, which is basically driving hardware sales through software features. And we went through this process that I just described. We stood up strategic pillars, and the strategic pillars were fairly similar for both Portal, which is our video conferencing product, and Oculus.
turns.zh: 在 Meta 有一个有趣的例子，我认为它说明了一个不同的观点，那就是...... (01:11:46)：基本上我是在为 Oculus Reality Labs 的几个产品增长团队制定产品策略，当时他们正在推出 Quest II。这是一个独立的耳机，然后是 Portal，这是我们的视频会议产品。我们成立了这些团队来追求产品增长，这基本上是通过软件功能推动硬件销售。我们经历了我刚才描述的这个过程。我们建立了战略支柱，Portal（我们的视频会议产品）和 Oculus 的战略支柱非常相似。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love Portal by the way. I was a big fan of... Sad that it's no longer around.
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，我喜欢《传送门》。我是……的忠实粉丝……遗憾的是它已经不复存在了。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: And that led to features that are known to everybody, like the Oculus Referrals Program, the Portal Memories Integration, where you see one of your Facebook memories on the Portal, sponsored ad in your Facebook feed. And also we had this section on the Facebook app, which is also from Facebook at the time, and then eventually also from Meta, which is these other products from the Facebook ecosystem. And all those came out of that effort. (01:13:01): And about 18 months into it, they actually had very different outcomes. So on one hand the Oculus effort was incredibly successful, and we graduated it into the VR division at Meta, and till today it continues to be an incredibly successful effort. The Portal effort actually didn't move the needle as much as we wanted to, and we sunset it, and we basically redeployed that team to other initiatives. And that's super interesting. Basically it was like the same strategy process. We got the nearly identical strategic pillars, but eventually completely different outcomes. (01:13:49): And I think that that illustrates the most important point about strategy, which is intrinsically strategy has no business value. It's basically a document with a few words. And I think it starts accumulating value as you generate business impact and results. And that happens when you actually test strategy with execution. (01:14:15): And so ultimately any strategy is only as good as the results it produces. And so one has to have the intellectual honesty, and the humility, and the courage to say when it's working and when it's not. And sometimes what happens is parts of your strategy might work, parts might not, and you have to pivot away from some and double down on some. But I do think there's that evaluation that's really critical and testing strategy with execution.
turns.zh: 这导致了众所周知的功能，例如 Oculus 推荐计划、Portal Memories Integration（门户记忆集成），您可以在 Portal 上看到您的 Facebook 记忆之一，在 Facebook feed 中看到赞助广告。我们在 Facebook 应用程序上也有这个部分，当时它也来自 Facebook，然后最终也来自 Meta，这是来自 Facebook 生态系统的其他产品。所有这些都是通过这种努力实现的。 (01:13:01)：大约 18 个月后，他们实际上得到了截然不同的结果。因此，一方面 Oculus 的努力非常成功，我们将其转移到 Meta 的 VR 部门，直到今天它仍然是一项非常成功的努力。门户网站的工作实际上并没有达到我们想要的效果，我们放弃了它，我们基本上将该团队重新部署到其他计划中。这非常有趣。基本上，这就像相同的战略流程。我们得到了几乎相同的战略支柱，但最终却完全不同的结果。 (01:13:49)：我认为这说明了战略最重要的一点，即战略本质上没有商业价值。它基本上是一个只有几句话的文档。我认为，当你产生业务影响和成果时，它就会开始积累价值。当你实际测试策略和执行时就会发生这种情况。 (01:14:15)：因此最终任何策略的好坏取决于它所产生的结果。因此，一个人必须具备理智上的诚实、谦逊和勇气，敢于说出什么时候有效，什么时候无效。有时，你的策略的一部分可能有效，一部分可能无效，你必须放弃某些策略，并在某些策略上加倍努力。但我确实认为评估非常关键，并且可以通过执行来测试策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a great point. Just a strategy sitting there in a doc is worthless, where the worth comes from, is it actually having impact and being successful. Makes me think about a product manager also, just a PM is not worth anything until they help you drive impact. (01:15:02): I think an important, to trickle down from that point, is that you don't want to spend too long just thinking about strategy, you want to spend as little time as possible to get to a strong hypothesis, basically to start learning if this is the right path. And so I love that your approach is like this middle ground between give it real time, but don't spend three, four or five months working on this one document that just maybe one day you'll use.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的观点。仅仅放在文档中的策略是毫无价值的，其价值来自于它是否真正产生影响并取得成功。让我也想到了产品经理，只有产品经理没有任何价值，除非他们能帮助你提高影响力。 (01:15:02)：我认为从这一点开始，一个重要的一点是，你不想花太长时间来思考策略，你想花尽可能少的时间来得到一个强有力的假设，基本上是开始学习这是否是正确的道路。所以我喜欢你的方法就像实时提供它之间的中间立场，但不要花三、四个或五个月的时间来处理这个可能有一天你会使用的文档。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly. (01:15:31): And there is room for a six-month process, which we'll get to in a moment. But for small S I wouldn't recommend more than two or three months.
turns.zh: 确切地。 (01:15:31)：还有为期六个月的过程的空间，我们稍后会讨论。但对于小S我不建议超过两三个月。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And again, small S strategy is for a couple of years out, not like Exactly. It's like a timeframe. Okay, cool. (01:15:47): Okay. Anything else along those lines of the examples of Meta or Zynga?
turns.zh: 再说一次，小S的策略是几年后的事，而不是像Exactly那样。这就像一个时间框架。好吧，酷。 (01:15:47)：好的。 Meta 或 Zynga 的例子还有其他类似的内容吗？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Those are pretty good lessons I would say.
turns.zh: 我想说，这些都是很好的教训。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, sweet. (01:15:56): So, let's talk about big-S strategy. When should you approach strategy this way and what are just the steps of it?
turns.zh: 好吧，亲爱的。 (01:15:56)：那么，我们来谈谈大S 策略。什么时候应该以这种方式实施策略？其步骤是什么？

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: So everything we've spoken about so far is what I would call small S, and it's very problem focused. It's basically what I call present forward. (01:16:17): It's like you have something, you have a product out there, it has a bunch of problems. How do we make it better for... What are the areas we tackle for maximum impact? Typically led by product managers. And there's this interesting quote by Elon Musk, which is, "Life has to be about more than just solving problems." And he says it in the context of the aspiration to become a multi-planetary species, but I think this is true of every company, big or small. And there needs to be an aspirational and cool component to strategy. And I call this big-S strategy. (01:16:56): I'll run through this at a higher level because I think this is a little bit more fluid in how you build the big-S strategy. And it typically takes longer, potentially up to about six months. The approach is a bit different from small S. And you start with the company mission and vision, and there is a little bit of groundwork that is done on long-term cultural trends, social trends, competitive trends, technological trends, and those are all the backdrop to trigger ideas. And what you do with that backdrop is you, again, do these leadership interviews, but with a different goal of generating long-term futures. (01:17:41): And some of the questions you can ask during these interviews are "What does a day in the life of a user look like in five years? What does the product look like in five to 10 years? Why is the world better in 10 years? And what is the most exciting version of that view?" And basically take all of that input and cluster it into I would say, three cohesive holes. (01:18:05): And what I mean by that is three, at least fairly distinct, descriptions of the future. So to give you almost a very simple example, imagine you doing big S for the future of travel. You could have a future that is talking all about fully autonomous travel, where there's very little human involvement in going from A to B. You could talk about another future where there's extreme speed, where you can get from A to B really fast across the world that is really fast. You could talk about a third where there is no travel, it's virtual travel, and you still have the feeling of travel, and you accomplish the same goals. (01:18:45): But those are different futures, they have different properties, like different elements to them. And once you generate those distinct futures, you actually generate prototypes with learning goals. And think of these prototypes as concept cars. And the automobile industry uses this notion of concept cars. Concept cars, the interesting thing about concept cars is they're never commercialized. They're often produced for inspiration, and to potentially take some part of them, like maybe a technology or a feature, and that is brought into mainstream production. (01:19:23): So think of these prototypes as these concept cars that really drive inspiration and potentially give you some small nuggets that you can run with. And then you start doing research with them with potential users, you answer key questions, and you uncover certain elements that resonate with people. So you eliminate a whole bunch of stuff, you combine a whole bunch of stuff, and you establish some winning components that are interesting. (01:19:48): And then what you do is you push stuff that is winning into the product, live product, testing. So this is actually something that you actually want to start testing your way into and understanding if it works from a scalable standpoint. And this whole thing is typically led not by the PM team, but by design and UXR. And intentionally it's a little bit more open-ended and green field. And it actually is a very different mind space that people have when they approach big. So the roadmap is really built through a combination of small-S and big-S work. And, for example, at VRChat, we are doing both small-S and big-S work, Lenny. And they are run as parallel work streams. The product management team is leading the charge of the small-S work, and the design team is leading the charge on the big-S work. And it's really exciting stuff. What's coming out of both work streams is really exciting and really different. And so we are building the bridge from both sides and both work streams ultimately flow into one roadmap. It's almost like two tributaries that ultimately merge into one river. That's how I would think about it.
turns.zh: 所以到目前为止我们所讨论的一切都是我所说的小S，而且它非常关注问题。这基本上就是我所说的“现在向前”。 (01:16:17)：就像你有一些东西，你有一个产品，但它有很多问题。我们如何让它变得更好......我们要解决哪些领域才能产生最大的影响？通常由产品经理领导。埃隆·马斯克（Elon Musk）有句有趣的名言：“生活不仅仅是解决问题。”他是在渴望成为一个多行星物种的背景下说这番话的，但我认为这对每个公司来说都是如此，无论大小。战略中需要有一个雄心勃勃且很酷的组成部分。我称之为大S 策略。 (01:16:56)：我会在更高的层面上讨论这个问题，因为我认为这对于构建大 S 策略来说更加流畅。通常需要更长的时间，可能长达六个月左右。这个做法和小S有点不一样，你从公司的使命和愿景开始，有一点基础，长期的文化趋势、社会趋势、竞争趋势、技术趋势，这些都是触发想法的背景。在这种背景下，你所做的就是再次进行这些领导力访谈，但目标不同，即创造长期未来。 (01:17:41)：在这些采访中您可以提出的一些问题是“五年后用户生活中的一天会是什么样子？五到十年后产品会是什么样子？为什么世界会在十年内变得更好？这种观点最令人兴奋的版本是什么？”基本上，将所有这些输入集中到我想说的三个有凝聚力的洞中。 (01:18:05)：我的意思是对未来的三种描述，至少是相当不同的描述。给你一个几乎非常简单的例子，想象一下你为未来的旅行做大S。你可以谈论完全自主旅行的未来，从 A 到 B 的过程中几乎不需要人类参与。你可以谈论另一个未来，那里有极快的速度，你可以非常快地穿越世界从 A 到 B。你可以谈论第三种，其中没有旅行，这是虚拟旅行，你仍然有旅行的感觉，并且你实现了相同的目标。 (01:18:45)：但这些是不同的未来，它们具有不同的属性，就像它们的不同元素一样。一旦你生成了这些不同的未来，你实际上就生成了具有学习目标的原型。并将这些原型视为概念车。汽车工业使用了概念车的概念。概念车，概念车的有趣之处在于它们从未商业化。它们通常是为了获得灵感而制作的，并可能采用其中的某些部分，例如一项技术或一项功能，并将其纳入主流生产。 (01:19:23)：因此，请将这些原型视为这些概念车，它们确实会激发灵感，并可能为您提供一些可以运行的小金块。然后你开始与潜在用户一起进行研究，回答关键问题，并发现某些能引起人们共鸣的元素。所以你消除了一大堆东西，你组合了一大堆东西，然后你建立了一些有趣的获胜组件。 (01:19:48)：然后你要做的就是将获胜的东西推入产品、实时产品、测试中。因此，这实际上是您真正想要开始测试的方法，并从可扩展的角度了解它是否有效。整个事情通常不是由 PM 团队领导，而是由设计和 UXR 领导。并且故意让它变得更加开放和绿色领域。事实上，当人们接近大的时候，他们的思维空间是非常不同的。因此，路线图实际上是通过小 S 和大 S 工作的结合来构建的。比如说，在 VRChat，我们同时做小 S 和大 S 的工作，Lenny。它们作为并行工作流运行。产品管理团队负责小S工作，设计团队负责大S工作。这确实是令人兴奋的事情。这两个工作流程的成果确实令人兴奋且截然不同。因此，我们正在从双方建立桥梁，两个工作流最终都会流入一个路线图。它几乎就像两条支流最终汇成一条河流。我就是这么想的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many things here that are so...
turns.zh: 这里有很多东西是那么...

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: That's how I would think about it.
turns.zh: 我就是这么想的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many things here that are so interesting. One is we've had this conversation on the podcast a couple of times, this point that people think and see the world differently. Some people are very open-minded and creative, and think big, blue sky people. Some people, me, just like, "What are we doing next? How do we move this metric? Let's talk about concrete things that we can do?" For this big S approach, I think what I'm hearing is make sure the people leading it are very open-minded, creative, blue sky type people. If you're the person that's like, "How will this move our metric?" Maybe you shouldn't be leading it and give someone else the reins. (01:21:40): Cool. And then with these timelines of doing both at once, it's probably hard to align them fully. So what I'm hearing is it's like these are kind of ongoing sometimes.
turns.zh: 这里有很多事情非常有趣。一是我们已经在播客上进行过几次这样的对话，这一点表明人们对世界的看法和看法有所不同。有些人思想非常开放，富有创造力，胸怀大志，蓝天白云。有些人，比如我，就会说，“我们接下来要做什么？我们如何移动这个指标？让我们谈谈我们可以做的具体事情？”对于这种大S方法，我认为我听到的是确保领导它的人是思想非常开放、有创造力、蓝天型的人。如果你是这样的人，“这将如何改变我们的指标？”也许你不应该领导它并把控制权交给别人。 (01:21:40)：酷。然后，由于同时进行这两项工作的时间表，可能很难将它们完全对齐。所以我听到的是，这些有时是持续进行的。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they'll both inform what you're doing. You don't need to have this perfect timeline of-
turns.zh: 他们都会告诉你你在做什么。你不需要有这个完美的时间表-

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: I agree to this. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我同意这一点。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. And the big thinking I love, because sometimes, you may experience this, designers often are like, "Oh, we just work on all this boring, incremental optimization stuff. I want to think bigger." Which is great, and this is a really good lever to allow for that in a contained environment. Cool. Let's just go crazy. Let's think about what this could be in the future. Still, let's make sure we're moving some metrics short-term, but let's give us opportunity to think big. And oftentimes the biggest ideas come out of that. So I love it's giving space for both types of thinking, thinking bigger and thinking long term. (01:22:30): Anything else about these two methods that might be interesting to share? Otherwise, I want to talk about AI a little bit, just how that impacts things and a couple other things.
turns.zh: 甜的。我喜欢宏大的思考，因为有时，你可能会经历这一点，设计师常常会说，“哦，我们只是致力于所有这些无聊的、增量优化的东西。我想思考更大的事情。”这太棒了，这是一个非常好的杠杆，可以在封闭的环境中实现这一点。凉爽的。让我们疯狂吧。让我们想想这在未来会发生什么。尽管如此，我们还是要确保短期内改变一些指标，但让我们有机会大胆思考。通常，最伟大的想法就是由此产生的。所以我喜欢它为两种思维方式提供空间，即更大的思考和长远的思考。 (01:22:30)：关于这两种方法还有什么值得分享的吗？除此之外，我想谈谈人工智能，它如何影响事物以及其他一些事情。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I'll end on one short sort of note on how this all feels when you do it, and then we can segue into AI-
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。最后我会用一个简短的注释来说明当你这样做时这一切的感受，然后我们可以继续讨论人工智能——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great, great.
turns.zh: 太棒了，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: ... Lenny. So I think that whether it's big S or small S, these are incredibly satisfying processes to go through in the end. So once you get to the end, they're incredibly deeply satisfying. But with anything in life that is very deeply satisfying at the end, they have a ton of challenge, frustration, and dead ends while you go through it where you kind of get a lot of self-doubt like, "Hey, will you ever reach the end?" And I just want to sort of normalize that. That's actually normal and I want people to expect that as they go through it. And I think that's what makes it even more rewarding when you get to that sort of point where you start to see things connecting. (01:23:33): The second thing is I would say that the person who's leading the charge on these efforts has to be really good at connecting diverse viewpoints and keeping them all moving forward. And it's not easy, it's very hard because sometimes you have people who take you in different directions and you have to keep it all hanging together. (01:23:57): So in terms of picking people who have that skill, who are good integrators, who are good connect the dots, I think it's critical for these to be successful. And in some ways low ego because it's not like... They do get to introduce their own ideas, but truly, it's about bringing the team together. So that's the skill that you should look for for these leads. (01:24:22): And then the third piece is I would say that I would just approach these with a little bit of a lighter touch and more playful sort of approach, because it's an intensive process, it's a long process. And people can get tired, they can find it grindy. So just having a little bit of playfulness along the way goes a long way in making it feel more tolerable for the people going through it. So those are some thoughts about either of these processes.
turns.zh: ……莱尼。所以我觉得无论是大S还是小S，最后经历这些都是非常令人满意的过程。所以一旦你读到最后，他们就会感到非常满足。但是，生活中任何最终令人非常满意的事情，都会有大量的挑战、挫折和死胡同，当你经历它时，你会产生很多自我怀疑，比如“嘿，你能到达终点吗？”我只是想让这种情况正常化。这实际上是正常的，我希望人们在经历它时对此有所期待。我认为这就是当你开始看到事物之间的联系时，它会变得更加有价值的原因。 (01:23:33)：第二件事是，我想说的是，领导这些努力的人必须非常擅长连接不同的观点并推动它们向前发展。这并不容易，也非常困难，因为有时有人会带你走向不同的方向，而你必须将这一切保持在一起。 (01:23:57)：因此，就挑选具有该技能的人、优秀的整合者、善于将各个点连接起来的人而言，我认为这些人的成功至关重要。在某些方面，他们的自我意识很低，因为这不像……他们确实可以介绍自己的想法，但实际上，这是为了让团队团结在一起。因此，这就是您应该为这些潜在客户寻找的技能。 (01:24:22)：第三点是我会说我会用更轻松的方式和更有趣的方式来处理这些问题，因为这是一个密集的过程，这是一个漫长的过程。人们可能会感到疲倦，他们会发现它很粗糙。因此，在这个过程中只要有一点乐趣，就能让正在经历这一过程的人们感觉更容易忍受。这些是关于这两个过程的一些想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was really important context, especially this will be frustrating throughout. It sounds really beautiful and great and smooth as you describe it. In reality, there's a lot of pain that goes into... Because you're making hard decisions. A lot of people have opinions, they have perspectives, there's data that's... Rarely is there clear answer from the beginning, so I think that's really important context. (01:25:08): I wanted to actually come back to your point you made about how Elon made this point about life shouldn't just be about solving problems. (01:25:32): I was actually at an interview with Zuck where he said the same thing. He's probably inspired by Elon. turns.zh: 这是非常重要的背景，尤其是这将在整个过程中令人沮丧。正如你所描述的那样，它听起来真的很漂亮、很棒、很流畅。事实上，有很多痛苦......因为你正在做出艰难的决定。很多人都有意见，有观点，有数据……很少从一开始就有明确的答案，所以我认为这是非常重要的背景。 (01:25:08)：我实际上想回到你的观点，即埃隆如何表明生活不应该只是解决问题。我认为这句话的一部分就像我们应该致力于那些令人敬畏、令人兴奋和鼓舞人心的事情，而不仅仅是立即解决痛苦。他非常擅长这一点，只是激励人们实现可能，我们应该思考比我们现在更宏大的想法。 (01:25:32)：实际上我在接受扎克的采访时他也说了同样的话。他可能受到埃隆的启发。他说，“我的职业生涯刚刚到了一个阶段，我想从事一些很棒的事情，那些令人敬畏的事情，而不仅仅是——

turns.speaker: Chandra Janakiraman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... another social feature." so I think that's a really important point. And there's a lot of power in that. People get really excited about holy moly, I did not imagine this is what Headspace could become, what VRChat could become, what Meta could become. It's just really powerful, getting people really inspired. And I love this process they shared of how to do that. (01:26:03): And I didn't actually summarize it, so I have it right here in front of me. I'll just share the five steps of the biggest process. So it's preparation, mission, you figure [inaudible 01:26:10] mission, vision, trends, interview people about where they think things are going.
